fullPassage:
In the United States, the practice of permitting aliens to vote could be seen as compatible with the idea of an exclusionary citizenship, but that is a hard balance to maintain. If the vote, of all rights, is in the hands of noncitizens, why should they not count as citizens, and the entire distinction between resident alien and citizen be abandoned? Indeed, something like this thought probably lay behind the disappearance of alien voting: with universal adult citizen suffrage after 1920, the only way to maintain an exclusionary kind of citizenship was to restrict the vote to citizens and not residents. But no theory of "active" democracy can countenance this distinction: the laws concerning our common life must be made by all those who are taking part in it, and residence is the only convincing test of whether someone is taking part — as is understood almost universally when it comes to questions of which citizens should have a voice in local government.

When people are asked what any painting hanging on a gallery wall means, no matter how strange it might appear, as is the case with most abstract-expressionist paintings, they tend to find meaning in it because it is located in a gallery. Consider a soda can found thrown away on a city street. If we were to come across this item on the street, we would no doubt view it as a piece of garbage or rubbish. But if we saw the very same object on a pedestal, displayed in an art gallery, signed by some artist, and given a title such as "Waste," then we would interpret its meaning in a vastly different way. We would, in fact, be inclined to interpret it as an artistic form, descrying a throw-away or materialistic society. Clearly, the can's location on a sidewalk versus its display on a pedestal in an art gallery will influence how we will interpret it.

The reliance on the computer as a model for the operations of the human mind may well prove to be as limited as an earlier fascination with behaviorism. Psychologists have already begun to recognize the flaws of the mind-as-computer metaphor. Some have turned to cultural anthropology as a way of understanding the factors outside any particular individual's brain that help the individual make sense out of the world. Others, such as Jerome Bruner, one of the founders of cognitive psychology, find that the computer analogy carries with it an unfortunate shift "from the construction of meaning to the processing of information." Bruner's reflections on the limits of the machine model lead him back to a humanistic emphasis on narrative and story-telling as essential ingredients in understanding human cognition, a fascinating intellectual journey that reveals both the power and the limits of computers as guides to the way we think.

In the escape that reading literature provides through vicarious identification and comparison with other lives, places, and times, we activate our imagination, that uniquely human ability to explore an alternative set of ideas and experiences that are outside our present environment and that may not even be real. As opposed to perception that receives and processes information from the outside world — light, sound, shape — and finds meaning in it — a sunset, a symphony, a house — in imagination, the process is reversed. Translating the words we read into what they signify, we populate an inner world in which imagery is created from the memory. For example, we read "house" and picture a representation of a house from memory. It is our imagination, the complex interweaving of perception and memory that literature activates, releasing a latent creativity that pleases. The writer may provide the blueprint, but the reader builds literature's many rooms, and like any satisfying occupation, literature gratifies our imaginative and creative abilities.

det.analysis:
❌ ① vicarious — 원문 일치. 대리적(vicarious) 동일시를 통해 문학이 탈출구를 제공한다는 맥락에 적절
❌ ② alternative — 원문 일치. 대안적(alternative) 아이디어와 경험을 탐색한다는 맥락에 적절
✅ ③ identical — 원문은 reversed(역전된). identical(동일한)로 바꾸면 지각과 상상의 과정이 동일하다는 뜻이 되어 'As opposed to perception'이라는 대비 맥락과 모순 ←정답
❌ ④ gratifies — 원문 일치. 문학이 상상력과 창의력을 만족시킨다(gratifies)는 맥락에 적절
det.tip: in imagination, the process is reversed(상상에서는 과정이 역전된다) — 지각의 반대 방향

questions.passage:
In the United States, the practice of permitting aliens to vote could be seen as compatible with the idea of an exclusionary citizenship, but that is a hard balance to maintain. If the vote, of all rights, is in the hands of noncitizens, why should they not count as citizens, and the entire distinction between resident alien and citizen be abandoned? Indeed, something like this thought probably lay behind the disappearance of alien voting: with universal adult citizen suffrage after 1920, the only way to maintain an exclusionary kind of citizenship was to restrict the vote to citizens and not residents. But no theory of "active" democracy can __________ this distinction: the laws concerning our common life must be made by all those who are taking part in it, and residence is the only convincing test of whether someone is taking part — as is understood almost universally when it comes to questions of which citizens should have a voice in local government.

When people are asked what any painting hanging on a gallery wall means, no matter how strange it might appear, as is the case with most abstract-expressionist paintings, they tend to find meaning in it because it is located in a gallery. Consider a soda can found thrown away on a city street. If we were to come across this item on the street, we would no doubt view it as a piece of garbage or rubbish. But if we saw the very same object on a pedestal, displayed in an art gallery, signed by some artist, and given a title such as "Waste," then we would interpret its meaning in a vastly different way. We would, in fact, be inclined to interpret it as an artistic form, descrying a throw-away or materialistic society. Clearly, the can's location on a sidewalk versus its display on a pedestal in an art gallery will influence how we will interpret it.

The reliance on the computer as a model for the operations of the human mind may well prove to be as limited as an earlier fascination with behaviorism. Psychologists have already begun to recognize the flaws of the mind-as-computer metaphor. Some have turned to cultural anthropology as a way of understanding the factors outside any particular individual's brain that help the individual make sense out of the world. Others, such as Jerome Bruner, one of the founders of cognitive psychology, find that the computer analogy carries with it an unfortunate shift "from the construction of meaning to the processing of information." Bruner's reflections on the limits of the machine model lead him back to a humanistic emphasis on narrative and story-telling as essential ingredients in understanding human cognition, a fascinating intellectual journey that reveals both the power and the limits of computers as guides to the way we think.

In the escape that reading literature provides through vicarious identification and comparison with other lives, places, and times, we activate our imagination, that uniquely human ability to explore an alternative set of ideas and experiences that are outside our present environment and that may not even be real. As opposed to perception that receives and processes information from the outside world — light, sound, shape — and finds meaning in it — a sunset, a symphony, a house — in imagination, the process is reversed. Translating the words we read into what they signify, we populate an inner world in which imagery is created from the memory. For example, we read "house" and picture a representation of a house from memory. It is our imagination, the complex interweaving of perception and memory that literature activates, releasing a latent creativity that pleases. The writer may provide the blueprint, but the reader builds literature's many rooms, and like any satisfying occupation, literature gratifies our imaginative and creative abilities.
questions.stem: 다음 글의 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?

det.analysis:
✅ ① countenance: 원문 일치. 능동적 민주주의 이론은 이 구별을 용인할(countenance) 수 없다는 맥락에 부합 ←정답

det.tip: no theory of active democracy can countenance this distinction — 능동적 민주주의는 이 구별을 용인할 수 없다

✅ ① favorable: favorable(호의적인/유리한)은 unfortunate(불행한/유감스러운)의 반의어 ←정답
❌ ② regrettable: regrettable(유감스러운)은 unfortunate와 유사한 동의어
❌ ③ harmful: harmful(해로운)은 unfortunate와 유사한 부정적 의미
❌ ④ neutral: neutral(중립적인)은 반의어가 아닌 다른 의미 축
det.tip: an unfortunate shift = 유감스러운 전환. favorable(유리한)이 정반대

questions.passage:
In the United States, the practice of permitting aliens to vote could be seen as compatible with the idea of an exclusionary citizenship, but that is a hard balance to maintain. If the vote, of all rights, is in the hands of noncitizens, why should they not count as citizens, and the entire distinction between resident alien and citizen be abandoned? Indeed, something like this thought probably lay behind the disappearance of alien voting: with universal adult citizen suffrage after 1920, the only way to maintain an exclusionary kind of citizenship was to restrict the vote to citizens and not residents. But no theory of "active" democracy can countenance this distinction: the laws concerning our common life must be made by all those who are taking part in it, and residence is the only convincing test of whether someone is taking part — as is understood almost universally when it comes to questions of which citizens should have a voice in local government.

When people are asked what any painting hanging on a gallery wall means, no matter how strange it might appear, as is the case with most abstract-expressionist paintings, they tend to find meaning in it because it is located in a gallery. Consider a soda can found thrown away on a city street. If we were to come across this item on the street, we would no doubt view it as a piece of garbage or rubbish. But if we saw the very same object on a pedestal, displayed in an art gallery, signed by some artist, and given a title such as "Waste," then we would interpret its meaning in a vastly different way. We would, in fact, be inclined to interpret it as an artistic form, descrying a throw-away or materialistic society. Clearly, the can's location on a sidewalk versus its display on a pedestal in an art gallery will influence how we will interpret it.

The reliance on the computer as a model for the operations of the human mind may well prove to be as limited as an earlier fascination with behaviorism. Psychologists have already begun to recognize the flaws of the mind-as-computer metaphor. Some have turned to cultural anthropology as a way of understanding the factors outside any particular individual's brain that help the individual make sense out of the world. Others, such as Jerome Bruner, one of the founders of cognitive psychology, find that the computer analogy carries with it an unfortunate shift "from the construction of meaning to the processing of information." Bruner's reflections on the limits of the machine model lead him back to a humanistic emphasis on narrative and story-telling as essential ingredients in understanding human cognition, a fascinating intellectual journey that reveals both the power and the limits of computers as guides to the way we think.

In the escape that reading literature provides through <u>vicarious</u> identification and comparison with other lives, places, and times, we activate our imagination, that uniquely human ability to explore an alternative set of ideas and experiences that are outside our present environment and that may not even be real. As opposed to perception that receives and processes information from the outside world — light, sound, shape — and finds meaning in it — a sunset, a symphony, a house — in imagination, the process is reversed. Translating the words we read into what they signify, we populate an inner world in which imagery is created from the memory. For example, we read "house" and picture a representation of a house from memory. It is our imagination, the complex interweaving of perception and memory that literature activates, releasing a latent creativity that pleases. The writer may provide the blueprint, but the reader builds literature's many rooms, and like any satisfying occupation, literature gratifies our imaginative and creative abilities.
questions.stem: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 vicarious와 의미가 가장 반대인 것은?

det.analysis:
❌ ① imaginary: imaginary(상상의)는 vicarious와 다른 의미 축. 대리 경험은 상상적일 수 있지만 반의어는 아님
✅ ② firsthand: firsthand(직접적인)는 vicarious(대리의/간접적인)의 정확한 반의어 ←정답
❌ ③ passive: passive(수동적인)는 능동/수동의 축으로 vicarious와 다른 의미 축
❌ ④ emotional: emotional(감정적인)은 vicarious와 관련 없는 의미 축
det.tip: vicarious identification = 대리적 동일시. firsthand(직접적인) 경험이 정반대

questions.stem: 다음 (A)와 (B)의 밑줄 친 part의 의미로 가장 적절한 것끼리 짝지은 것은?

det.korean: (A) taking part=참여하다, (B) a part of=~의 일부/부분
det.analysis:
❌ ① 역할 — 역할: (A)는 '역할'보다 '참여'가 맥락에 부합, (B)도 '역할'보다 '부분'이 맥락에 부합
❌ ② 부분 — 참여: (A)(B) 의미가 뒤바뀜
❌ ③ 참여 — 참여: (B)는 '참여'가 아닌 '부분/일부'가 맥락에 맞음
✅ ④ 참여 — 부분: (A) taking part in it=공동 생활에 참여하다, (B) a part of this creative process=창의적 과정의 일부 ←정답
det.tip: take part in=참여하다 / a part of=~의 일부. 같은 단어 part가 다른 의미로 쓰임

questions.stem: 다음 영영 정의에 해당하는 단어로 가장 적절한 것은? "the state of being a citizen with its rights and duties"

det.korean: 시민으로서의 권리와 의무를 가진 상태 → citizenship(시민권)
det.analysis:
❌ ① residency: residency(거주권)는 거주 상태이지 시민의 권리와 의무를 의미하지 않음
✅ ② citizenship: citizenship(시민권)은 '시민으로서의 권리와 의무를 가진 상태'라는 정의에 정확히 부합 ←정답
❌ ③ democracy: democracy(민주주의)는 정치 체제이지 개인의 시민 상태가 아님
❌ ④ suffrage: suffrage(선거권/참정권)는 투표할 권리만을 의미하며 시민 상태 전체를 포괄하지 않음
det.tip: citizenship = the state of being a citizen with its rights and duties

questions.passage: Psychologists have already begun to recognize the flaws of the mind-as-computer metaphor. Some have turned to cultural anthropology as a way of __________ (understand) the factors outside any particular individual's brain that help the individual make sense out of the world.
questions.stem: 다음 글의 빈칸에 괄호 안의 단어를 알맞은 형태로 바꿔 쓰시오. (영어로)

det.korean: 이해하는 방법으로 — a way of + 동명사(V-ing)
det.analysis:
a way of 뒤에는 동명사(-ing)가 와야 하므로 understand → understanding.
구문: a way of understanding the factors = 요인들을 이해하는 방법
det.tip: a way of + V-ing(~하는 방법) — 전치사 of 뒤에 동명사

questions.passage: It is our imagination, the complex interweaving of perception and memory that literature activates, __________ (release) a latent creativity that pleases.
questions.stem: 다음 글의 빈칸에 괄호 안의 단어를 알맞은 형태로 바꿔 쓰시오. (영어로)

det.analysis:
주절(It is our imagination ~ that literature activates)에 이어 분사구문이 와야 하므로 release → releasing.
구문: releasing a latent creativity = 잠재적 창의성을 풀어주면서(분사구문, 동시 동작)
det.tip: 분사구문(현재분사): 주절의 주어(literature)가 activate하면서 동시에 release하는 것 → releasing

questions.stem: 다음 글의 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?

❌ ① suffrage: suffrage(선거권)는 투표할 권리이지 참여 여부의 기준이 아님

det.tip: residence is the only convincing test of whether someone is taking part — 거주가 유일한 설득력 있는 기준

questions.stem: 다음 글의 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?

det.analysis:
✅ ① blueprint: 원문 일치. 작가가 청사진(blueprint)을 제공하지만 독자가 문학의 많은 방을 짓는다는 비유적 맥락에 부합 ←정답
❌ ② imagination: imagination(상상력)은 독자의 능력이지 작가가 제공하는 것이 아님
❌ ③ perception: perception(지각)은 외부 정보를 받아들이는 과정이지 작가가 제공하는 것이 아님
❌ ④ memory: memory(기억)는 독자의 내면 자원이지 작가가 제공하는 것이 아님
det.tip: The writer may provide the blueprint, but the reader builds literature's many rooms — 작가=설계도, 독자=건축
